User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: I can help you get organized. Below is a practical checklist you can use to prepare for your next steps with Lisa Park and for any upcoming court appearance. These are general preparation suggestions — your attorney is the best source for legal strategy, so use this list to guide your conversation with her.

1) Quick context check (confirm these with Lisa)
- What type of hearing will the court schedule next (status conference, scheduling conference, motion hearing, preliminary injunction, trial setting, etc.)?
- Is the hearing in federal district court for the Western District of Washington (King County venue) a remote appearance or in-person?
- Will you be expected to testify, or will Lisa argue/appear for you?
- Are there any pending motions or deadlines the court will address at the next hearing?

2) Documents to bring (collect and organize these now)
Core contract and transaction evidence
- The executed NDA/contract (original or a clear copy) and any amendments or addenda.
- Proof of signing/receipt (emails confirming delivery, timestamps, delivery receipts).
Communications
- All communications with the former landlord about the NDA/contract and performance (emails, texts, letters), arranged in chronological order.
- Any demand letters you sent and the landlord’s responses.
Performance & breach evidence
- Documents showing the landlord stopped performing (e.g., notices of nonperformance, failed repairs, withheld services, invoices showing unmet obligations).
- Records showing you performed your obligations (payments, compliance, deliveries).
Financial/damages proof
- Rent ledgers, bank statements, invoices, receipts, estimates for damages/mitigation costs, spreadsheets that calculate monetary damages or losses.
Supporting evidence
- Photos, inspection reports, work orders, repair estimates, receipts for mitigation, and any contemporaneous notes.
Witness and testimonial materials
- Contact info and brief statements or declarations from witnesses (e.g., neighbors, contractors) who observed relevant events.
Court filings and procedural documents
- Copies of court filings already submitted: complaint, exhibits, affidavits/declarations, discovery responses, certificates of service, any orders the court has issued.
Expert materials (if applicable)
- Any expert reports, invoices, or qualifications you’ve received or expect to use.
Exhibit organization & logistics
- An exhibit list/index with exhibit numbers and short descriptions.
- Multiple courtesy copies of exhibits: one for the court, one for opposing counsel, and one for you/your attorney (or as Lisa requests).
- USB drive with PDF copies of all exhibits (labeled), and a printed binder with tabbed exhibits.
Administrative items
- Photo ID, contact info for counsel and witnesses, calendar availability, and any filings to present to the judge (proposed order, proposed scheduling/docket plan).

3) How to organize the materials for Lisa and the court
- Create a one-page timeline (date → short fact) covering the key events from contract signing to the present.
- Prepare an exhibit index that maps each fact/claim to exhibit numbers.
- Produce a short damages summary (one page) showing how you calculated losses and what relief you’re asking for.
- Make a “hearing binder”: intro page, timeline, exhibit index, copies of the top 10 exhibits, filings, and the proposed order.

4) Questions to ask Lisa Park (use these in your next call/meeting)
Procedural & scheduling
- What exactly will the court address at the next calendar call/hearing?
- What filings (if any) must be submitted before the hearing (briefs, exhibit lists, proposed orders) and what are their deadlines?
- Will we need to file witness lists, exhibit lists, or proposed findings in advance? How many days before the hearing?
Evidence & witnesses
- Which documents do you (Lisa) want me to bring or highlight?
- Will any witness testimony be used at the hearing? If so, who will testify and in what order?
- Do we need witness declarations or affidavits filed in advance?
Strategy & messaging
- What is our principal legal theory (what relief are we asking for)?
- What are the key facts I should emphasize if the judge asks me questions?
- What are the main weaknesses the other side will raise and how should I respond?
Courtroom logistics & preparation
- Will I need to appear and possibly testify? If yes, can we do a prep session/mock Q&A?
- Dress code, arrival time, courtroom protocols for this judge/court.
Settlement & negotiation
- Are settlement talks advisable now? If the judge asks about settlement, how should I respond?
Practicalities
- Do you want copies of the timeline/exhibit index now? What format do you prefer (PDF, Word, printed binder)?
- How long will the hearing likely last, and how much of that will involve factual testimony vs. argument?

5) What to say at the hearing — short scripts and tips
If you’re not testifying (Lisa speaks):
- Be present, attentive, quiet, and let Lisa speak. Provide documents to Lisa in the order she requests.
If you are asked to speak or testify:
- Keep answers short and factual. Start with your name and role briefly. Example opening: “My name is [Your Name]. I signed the NDA on [date]. The landlord stopped performing on [date], and I notified them on [dates]. I lost [concise damages summary].”
- Use the timeline and reference exhibit numbers: “As shown in Exhibit 3, on [date] the landlord acknowledged [fact].”
- When asked about relief: state the remedy succinctly — e.g., “We are asking the Court to [describe relief: enforce the NDA, award damages of $X, enter injunctive relief, etc.], and the basis is [one-line legal basis].”
Tips during the hearing
- Don’t volunteer extra information. Answer only what you’re asked.
- If you don’t know or don’t remember, say so — then offer to check the record and provide it through counsel.
- If the judge asks a procedural question you don’t know, defer politely to your attorney: “I’d like to defer to Ms. Park on the procedural question, your Honor.”
- Remain calm, professional, and concise.

6) Practical next steps to be “court ready”
- Assemble binder, timeline, exhibit index, and a damages one-pager.
- Send the materials to Lisa at least as early as she requests (or now if she asked).
- Schedule a prep call with Lisa for witness prep (if you will testify) and go over the script.
- Confirm hearing logistics with Lisa (date, time, location or Zoom link, judge’s chambers preferences).
- Check local Federal Rules and the judge’s standing orders (Lisa will likely handle this but ask if there are special formatting or exhibit requirements).

7) If you want, I can:
- Draft an email to Lisa Park (Park Legal Group) summarizing these documents and requesting a prep meeting — include the checklist and propose dates/times.
- Create a printable one-page timeline or exhibit index template you can fill in.
- Create a concise “what to say” script tailored to your exact facts (if you give the key dates and the relief you’ll seek).

8) One last note on confidentiality and sharing
- These suggestions are for preparation only. Follow Lisa Park’s strategy and any advice she provides for courtroom statements.
- If you’d like help drafting the email to Lisa or preparing the timeline/exhibit index, tell me the exact points you want included and I’ll draft it for you (I won’t send anything without your permission).

Would you like me to draft the email to Lisa Park now with the checklist and a request for a prep session? If yes, tell me:
- Her email address (or say “use my usual address on file”),
- Any dates/times you’re available for a prep meeting, and
- The top 3 facts and the relief you intend to seek (damages amount or injunction), so I can tailor the draft.
